newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bonds see no fret from housing data leap.
newsitem.headline: Australia bonds see no fret from housing data leap.

text.p: *Australian bond yields were just below their initial highs after April housing finance came in in line with expectations, albeit up 12.2 percent.
*NAB survey shows business confidence still falling.
Australian bond yields were just below their initial highs after April housing finance data came in line with median expectations, up 12.2 percent.

Analysts had anticipated a large rise following private data on commitments from major banks rising 15 percent in the April period, and the market is more cautious on the outcome of Thursday's labour force data with regard to future policy.

"There is absolutley no implications for monetary policy (from the housing data)," said Annette Beacher, senior economist at Citibank Australia, adding that the Reserve Bank and the Treasury have made it clear they are pursuing growth.

"(The authorities) need data like this to get growth and given what mortgage rates have done, this is the sort of figures we expect to see. The financial markets had a quick look at the data and moved on," Beacher added.
In contrast, National Australia Bank's monthly Australian business survey released at the same time as the housing data showed a further fall in confidence.

The NAB said that recent falls in interest rates had failed to arrest a decline in business confidence, and while conditions varied across sectors, a generalised pick-up had yet to occur with underlying annual growth remaining around 2.5/3.0 percent.

Bond yields had risen in early trading, partly reflecting the softer close in U.S. Treasuries and as the local market continued to digest the implications of the RBA's cut in commercial bank's prime asset ratios to three from six percent.
Turnover was boosted by the roll-over of futures contracts to September from June with bills closing out on Thursday and three and 10-year bonds on Monday.

The May labour force report is due on Thursday and employment is forecast to rise 15,000, while the unemployment rate is expected to remain at 8.7 percent, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

The local market gave up some of Tuesday's narrowing trend to the dollar bloc. This was particularly notable at the long end against Canada, which was boosted by foreign buying and spread narrowing trades to the U.S. The 30-year U.S./Canada spread is now trading around parity.
